items.title: R to @NOELreports: An extensive update on Sloviansk
items.summary:
An extensive update on Sloviansk
NOELREPORTS 🇪🇺 🇺🇦 (@NOELreports)
Sloviansk axis update - 30-09-2026
Before getting into the recent changes, some context is needed. Our map in this area had not been updated for some time, so the Russian advance shown here did not all happen after the beginning of June. A fair amount of ground east and northeast of Rai-Oleksandrivka had already been lost earlier, particularly south east of Kalenyky and the areas east of Fedorivka Druha-Nykyforivka. By early June, however, the situation started moving much faster. Russian troops were pressing west from Kalenyky and Kryva Luka, while farther south another axis was developing around Lypivka, Nykyforivka and Fedorivka Druha. Rai-Oleksandrivka increasingly sat between these two areas of pressure. Russian troops entered parts of the village during June, but control was never as straightforward as some of the early claims suggested. Ukrainian units remained active around Rai and, at times, inside it. The surrounding forests and treelines gradually turned into a wide contested area where confirmed presence did not necessarily mean firm control.
By July, the fighting was moving beyond Rai itself. From Kalenyky and Kryva Luka, Russian assault groups worked toward Pyskunivka and through the forests south of the Siverskyi Donets. That brought increasing pressure on Starodubivka and the northeastern approaches to Mykolaivka. South of Rai, Russian forces were also expanding around Fedorivka Druha, Nykyforivka and the canal, giving them another way of approaching the area behind Rai. This is where the front became particularly difficult to map. Small Russian groups often moved well ahead of their main positions through the forests, while Ukrainian troops were still present in pockets that had already been coloured Russian on some maps. By the end of July, Russian troops were appearing close enough to Mykolaivka for the situation to become much more serious. The danger was obvious: pressure from Pyskunivka and Kryva Luka from the northeast, combined with the push through Rai from the southeast, could eventually put Mykolaivka between two Russian axes.
That danger probably peaked during August. Russian troops strengthened their positions around Kryva Luka and reached the southeastern side of Pyskunivka, while other groups moved west from Rai-Oleksandrivka through the forests toward the southern and southeastern approaches to Mykolaivka. Fighting also continued around Orikhuvatka, with pressure still present farther south around Fedorivka Druha. Russia was able to get small groups surprisingly far forward, but keeping them there was another matter. Supply routes through the forests were vulnerable to Ukrainian drones, and isolated positions were regularly hit by local counterattacks. Orikhuvatka showed how messy the situation had become. Russian sources claimed it, but later evidence still showed Ukrainian positions in the area. Rai was much the same. Russian troops clearly held substantial parts of the village at different points during the summer, but Ukrainian positions remained nearby and the actual line often ran through individual streets, treelines or sections of forest rather than around the settlement as a whole.
The first real change came in September. Ukrainian troops started showing up farther east again around Rai-Oleksandrivka and Orikhuvatka, and around 10 to 12 September the local counterattacks turned into something larger. Ukrainian units moved back into central Rai and began attacking Russian positions north and east of the village. The contested area toward Mykolaivka started shrinking. Farther north, Ukrainian forces around Starodubivka and Pyskunivka also put pressure on Russian positions south of the Siverskyi Donets, while attacks from the Ozerne side increased the pressure around Kryva Luka. It would be wrong to read them as every forest suddenly being cleared. Russian groups remained in parts of the area, sometimes well forward of the more established positions. What changed was that those groups were now operating under much greater pressure, especially west of Kalenyky.
The Ukrainian Vivaldi offensive around Lyman and Yampil, and the recapture of Dibrova, added another problem for Russia on the northern flank. Sloviansk axis update - 30-09-2026
Before getting into the recent changes, some context is needed. Our map in this area had not been updated for some time, so the Russian advance shown here did not all happen after the beginning of June. A fair amount of ground east and northeast of Rai-Oleksandrivka had already been lost earlier, particularly south east of Kalenyky and the areas east of Fedorivka Druha-Nykyforivka. Russian troops were pressing west from Kalenyky and Kryva Luka, while farther south another axis was developing around Lypivka, Nykyforivka and Fedorivka Druha. Rai-Oleksandrivka increasingly sat between these two areas of pressure. Russian troops entered parts of the village during June, but control was never as straightforward as some of the early claims suggested. Ukrainian units remained active around Rai and, at times, inside it. The surrounding forests and treelines gradually turned into a wide contested area where confirmed presence did not necessarily mean firm control.

items.title: "Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment. Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to 'destroy pretty much the entire economy'. 'What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,' he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks... The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27 bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.
